_note: Authored general guidance for this demo. Not legal or carrier advice; requirements vary by carrier, trade lane and commodity.

entries.topic: Documents needed to make a booking
entries.answer: For a booking request you normally give the shipper and consignee, origin and destination, a commodity description, the container type and quantity, an estimated cargo weight and the sailing you want. After the booking is confirmed you submit shipping instructions and the verified gross mass, and prepare the commercial invoice, packing list and any export declaration your origin country requires. Exact requirements differ by carrier and commodity, so confirm with the carrier.

Shipping instructions tell the carrier what to print on the bill of lading: shipper, consignee, notify party, cargo description, marks, package count, weight and container numbers. They must reach the carrier before the documentation cut-off of the sailing; the carrier then issues a draft bill of lading for you to check.

VGM is the verified gross mass of a packed container: cargo, packing and securing material plus the container tare. Under the SOLAS convention a packed container may not be loaded without it. The shipper named on the bill of lading is responsible for declaring it, either by weighing the packed container or by weighing all contents and adding the tare. It must be submitted before the VGM cut-off of the sailing.

entries.topic: Cut-offs and what happens if you miss one
entries.answer: The CY cut-off is the latest time a laden container can be gated in at the terminal for a sailing. The documentation cut-off is the latest time for shipping instructions, and the VGM cut-off is the latest time for the verified gross mass. If you miss one, the container is usually moved to a later sailing and extra charges may apply; contact the carrier as early as possible.

Send an amendment request to the carrier with the booking number and the fields to change, such as quantity, container type, sailing or cargo details. Amendments are subject to space and equipment, and changes after the documentation cut-off or after gate-in may be refused or charged.

Ask the carrier to cancel using the booking number. Cancelling close to the sailing, or not delivering the container at all, can attract a cancellation or no-show fee depending on the terms of the carrier.

Dangerous goods need carrier approval before the booking is confirmed. Expect to provide a dangerous goods declaration, a safety data sheet and the classification under the IMDG Code: UN number, proper shipping name, class and packing group. Some commodities are not accepted on some vessels or ports.

entries.topic: Original bill of lading, sea waybill and telex release
entries.answer: An original bill of lading is a document of title: an original must be surrendered to the carrier before the cargo is released. A sea waybill is not a document of title; cargo is released to the named consignee without presenting an original. A telex release means the originals were surrendered at origin and the carrier tells the destination office to release the cargo without them.

On a direct service the container stays on the same vessel from origin to destination. With transshipment it is discharged at an intermediate port and loaded onto another vessel, which usually adds time and one more point where delay can occur.

A certificate of origin states where the goods were made. Whether you need one depends on the customs rules of the destination country, on whether you claim a preferential duty rate under a trade agreement, and on what the buyer or the letter of credit asks for. It is issued by a chamber of commerce or an authorised body, not by the carrier, and is not required to place a booking.

Published sailing dates and cut-offs are estimates and can change with weather, port congestion or vessel swaps. This demo uses a static fictional sample with a stated as-of date, so always confirm dates and cut-offs with the carrier before acting on them.

For reefer cargo the booking must state the set temperature and, where relevant, the ventilation and humidity settings. Check that the carrier offers reefer plugs on the sailing, and pre-cool the cargo rather than the empty container unless the carrier advises otherwise.
